about: Fact sheet for the Data page: the real-world numbers behind HOME BY SEVEN. Each fact has a stable id, a value and unit, one of the four labels (measured, computed, rule, story; src/lib/labels.ts), one source link, the words on that page (quote) and, for computed facts, the calculation. The sentence the player reads is the i18n key data.fact.<id> in src/i18n/<lang>/data.json (written by Aminjon; drafts in docs/specs/2026-11-14-facts.md). Numbers checked by Sarvar. Every source was fetched on the date below. Validated by src/lib/facts.test.ts.

facts.label: measured
facts.where: Walking and jumping physics (Moon gravity in CLAUDE.md, docs/TASKS.md §4.9)

facts.label: computed
facts.quote: the gravity on the surface of the Moon is one-sixth of Earth's, which is why in footage of moonwalks, astronauts appear to almost bounce across the surface.
facts.calc: Jump height = v² ÷ 2g, so the same take-off speed lifts you 9.80 ÷ 1.62 = 6.05 times higher (gravity values from the NSSDCA Moon Fact Sheet).

facts.label: measured

source.title: How Far Away Is the Moon? (NASA Space Place)

facts.quote: The Moon is an average of 238,855 miles (384,400 km) away. How far away is that? That's 30 Earths.
facts.where: Data page; distance behind the radio delay and Earth's size in the sky

facts.label: computed

source.title: Laser Beams Reflected Between Earth and Moon Boost Science (NASA)

facts.quote: By measuring how long it takes laser light to bounce back — about 2.5 seconds on average — researchers can calculate the distance between Earth laser stations and Moon reflectors
facts.calc: Radio travels at the speed of light: 2.5 s there and back ÷ 2 ≈ 1.3 s one way; also 384,400 km ÷ 299,792 km/s = 1.28 s.

facts.label: computed
facts.quote: The Moon takes about one month to orbit Earth (27.3 days to complete a revolution, but 29.5 days to change from new moon to new moon). … It takes a little more than two additional days for sunlight to hit the Moon in the same way it did on day zero.
facts.calc: One lap of the Sun around the Moon's sky = new moon to new moon = 29.5 days; 360° ÷ 29.5 days ≈ 12° a day, the Sun's daily step in sky.json.
facts.where: Sun moves ~12° a day (src/engine/sky.json sun_az_deg, src/scene/Stage.tsx fallback, docs/layout.md)

facts.label: computed

source.title: Shadows near the Moon's South Pole (NASA Science)

facts.quote: At the Moon's North and South Poles, the Sun is never more than 1.5° above or below the horizon. … At the Moon's poles, the Sun is always near the horizon, and the shadows are perpetually long
facts.calc: Sky mechanics: 'Unlike Earth's 23.5-degree tilt, the Moon is tilted only 1.5 degrees on its axis' (https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/nasas-artemis-base-camp-on-the-moon-will-need-light-water-elevation/), so near the pole the Sun skims the horizon. The game keeps the Sun at 1.5° (a game rule: sky.json sun_el_deg); at 1.5° a shadow is 1 ÷ tan 1.5° ≈ 38 times longer than the object.

facts.label: computed
facts.calc: Earth's width seen from the Moon: 2 × 6,378 km ÷ 384,400 km = 0.0332 rad = 1.9°. The Moon seen from Earth: 2 × 1,737.4 km ÷ 384,400 km = 0.52° (Moon Fact Sheet), so Earth looks about 3.7 times wider.
facts.where: Earth in the sky (sky.json earth_el_deg, features.earthOfTheDay)

facts.label: measured
facts.quote: Surface pressure (night): 3 x 10-15 bar (2 x 10-12 torr)
facts.note: Earth's air at sea level is about 1 bar. Almost no air: no sound outside, a black sky, almost no ambient light.
facts.where: Silence outside (.claude/rules/hud-text.md, Sound), black sky and ambient ≈ 0 (src/scene/Light.tsx)

facts.label: measured

source.title: Ten Cool Things Seen in the First Year of LRO (NASA Scientific Visualization Studio)

facts.quote: Diviner, LRO's temperature instrument, found a place in the floor of the moon's Hermite Crater that was detected to be -415 degrees Fahrenheit (-248 Celsius) making it the coldest temperature measured anywhere in the solar system. For comparison, scientists believe that Pluto's surface only gets down to about -300 degrees Fahrenheit (-184 Celsius). Extremely cold regions similar to the one in Hermite Crater were found at the bottoms of several permanently shaded craters at the lunar south pole

facts.label: measured
facts.quote: As planned, LCROSS and its Centaur stage impacted the Moon on Oct. 9, 2009. … The Centaur then crashed onto the surface of the Moon at 11:31 UT in the Cabeus crater at the lunar south pole. … They also confirmed that in some places the water on the south pole is in the form of pure ice crystals.

facts.label: measured
facts.quote: LRO has been studying the Moon from up close since 2009, making it the longest-lived lunar orbiting mission ever. The orbiter has mapped the Moon's surface and measured its temperature, composition, and radiation environment
facts.note: CRaTER is LRO's radiation instrument: 'The instrument comprises tissue-equivalent plastic and silicon detectors to determine the effects of radiation on human tissue.' (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/experiment/display.action?id=2009-031A-06). The game's archive is CRaTER-D1D2 via NASA OSDR RadLab, 2012–2024.
facts.where: Radiation level and ratio on every day (src/engine/weeks.json, ui.truth.*)

facts.label: measured

source.title: LRO CRaTER hourly dose rate, NASA OSDR RadLab API (request for the week of 25 Oct 2021)

facts.quote: Hourly CRaTER-D1D2 absorbed_dose_rate: the 25th percentile of the 600 readings from 28 Sep to 24 Oct 2021 is 12.43 µGy/h (re-computed from this request on 2026-11-14).
facts.note: Range of the calm value (normal_uGy_h) over the 14 weeks in src/engine/weeks.json: 4.86 (2024-05-08) to 13.37 (2020-06-01); every week's request URL is in weeks.json sources. Measured in lunar orbit behind thin shielding, never a dose at the base.
facts.where: ★★★ radiation badge in µGy/h; the calm value that ratios are divided by (weeks.json normal_uGy_h)

facts.label: measured

source.title: LRO CRaTER hourly dose rate, NASA OSDR RadLab API (request for the week of 20 Jan 2012)

facts.quote: CRaTER-D1D2 hourly readings on 24 Jan 2012: 13,803 to 61,829 µGy/h (re-fetched 2026-11-14).
facts.note: Week 2012-01-20, day 5 (24 Jan 2012): day mean 32,395 µGy/h ÷ calm value 8.77 µGy/h = 3692, the largest ratio in weeks.json (weeks.json method: rows are stamped at the end of their hour).

facts.label: rule

source.title: NOAA Space Weather Scales (NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center)

facts.quote: Solar Radiation Storms — Physical measure (Flux level of >= 10 MeV particles): S 1 10, S 2 10^2, S 3 10^3, S 4 10^4, S 5 10^5
facts.note: The game's levels 0–4 start at 2, 10, 100 and 1,000 times normal (docs/rules.md, Radiation). The cut points are a game rule shaped like NOAA's scale, where each level is ten times the one before; the game applies them to the CRaTER ratio, not to particle flux.

facts.label: measured

source.title: DONKI flare record FLR 18096 (CCMC, NASA Goddard)

facts.quote: Intensity : X1.0 class … Start Time : 2021-10-28T15:17:00Z Peak Time : 2021-10-28T15:35:00Z End Time : 2021-10-28T15:48:00Z Detecting Spacecraft GOES-P: EXIS
facts.note: DONKI is the space-weather event database of the Community Coordinated Modeling Center; the game reads its flare (FLR) and particle (SEP) records for each week. Same flare in the API: https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI-API/get/FLR?startDate=2021-10-25&endDate=2021-10-31
facts.where: Flare alert card, week 2021-10-25 day 4 (weeks.json flares, public/data/media/2021-10-25/manifest.json)

facts.label: measured

source.title: SDO data channels (NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory)

facts.quote: 131 Å — Fe xx, xxiii — Flaring regions — 7.0, 7.2
facts.note: 131 Å = 13.1 nm, extreme ultraviolet that eyes cannot see; log T 7.0 = about 10 million kelvin. The colours of the picture are false colour.
facts.where: Sun pictures before and at the flare (public/data/media/<week>/sdo-*.webp)

facts.label: measured
facts.quote: VIIRS is one of five instruments onboard the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (NPP) satellite … Swath Dimensions: 3000km, nearly global coverage every day
facts.note: The Earth pictures of week 2021-10-25 are the GIBS layer VIIRS_SNPP_CorrectedReflectance_TrueColor for each day of the week (manifest.json).
facts.where: Earth of that day on the globe (public/data/media/<week>/earth-<date>.webp)
